summary: Longshadow is a web app that shows where the Sun and Earth sit above the real horizon at any landing site on the Moon, on any date. At the lunar south pole the Sun never climbs more than about 1.5 degrees, so every hill decides if a lander has power. Earth sits low too, so hills also decide if it can talk to mission control. We compute the real skyline of each site from NASA LOLA terrain and the real Sun and Earth positions from JPL's DE440 ephemeris. Then we show it three ways: the view from the lander, a 3D map with live shadows, and a timeline of power and radio windows. A comparison page tests a full year of landing dates for many sites at once, so a planner can see in seconds which site still works when a launch slips. Our Sun and Earth angles match the JPL Horizons System to within 0.1 arcsecond, and our sunlight numbers match a published NASA Goddard study. It matters because picking a polar site and date is slow with today's tools, and a wrong pick means a lander with no power.
details:
What it does

- Navigator. Pick one of 29 ready sites (the 13 Artemis III candidate regions, Shackleton rim, the south pole, IM-1, IM-2, LCROSS, Chandrayaan-3, the six Apollo sites and more) or type any coordinates or drop a pin on the map. Pick a date and time, or press play.

- View from the lander. A panorama with the real skyline, drawn from laser altimeter data, and the Sun and Earth at their true size. You see the Sun slide behind a ridge and Earth dip under the hills.

- 3D Moon. The south pole in 3D with shadows cast live from the terrain toward the true Sun direction. A second mode lights every place that can see Earth right now.

- Windows. A timeline shows when solar power and the direct link to Earth are on and off, to the minute, with a countdown to the next sunset and the next loss of signal. You choose what counts: any Sun, half the disk or the full disk, and how many degrees Earth must clear the skyline.

- Compare sites and dates. Set the mission: length of stay, how long the lander survives without power, how much power and link it needs. Each site gets a one year calendar of landing dates that work. Click any date to test all sites for that day.

- For everyone. A short story page explains why the south pole is hard, using the same live data. Every number has a plain sentence next to it, like "The whole Sun is clear of the terrain."

How it works

1. Sun and Earth: apparent positions seen from the Moon come from JPL DE440 through NASA's SPICE toolkit, in the same Moon frame as the terrain maps. Light time and aberration are included. The app carries a table for 2020 to 2050 and interpolates it. The interpolation error is under 0.02 arcsecond.

2. Terrain: LOLA elevation maps from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, 5 m per pixel around the candidate regions, 20 m down to 80°S and 240 m down to 60°S.

3. Skyline: from each site we send 1,440 rays out to 500 km over the curved Moon. The highest terrain along each ray is the skyline in that direction. We store it for 2 m and 10 m above the ground.

4. Windows: the Sun is a disk half a degree wide that grazes the skyline. We cut the disk into strips, clip them by the skyline and weight by limb darkening. That gives the share of sunlight from 0 to 100 percent. The link is available when Earth's centre clears the skyline by the chosen margin.

5. Site search: for each Artemis III region our pipeline searches NASA's 5 m map for the best lit spot with a slope under 10 degrees, within 6 km of the published centre. On the Connecting Ridge it lands on one of the areas published by NASA Goddard.

How we checked it

- Against the JPL Horizons System: 8 sites, one year, 2,928 comparisons of Sun and Earth angles. Largest difference 0.098 arcsecond. For the Sun alone 0.011 arcsecond.

- Against Barker et al. 2021 (NASA Goddard): sunlight at 7 areas on the Connecting Ridge at two heights. 14 of 14 of our averages fall inside the published range.

- The browser code is tested against the Python and SPICE pipeline for a full year at every site with terrain. They agree within 0.15 percent.

- The LCROSS impact site comes out with zero sunlight all year, as a permanently shadowed crater should.

Benefits

- Mission planners can compare sites and dates in seconds and see the effect of a schedule slip at once.

- It shows why a few metres of mast height or a short move changes the power budget.

- Teachers and students can see why the lunar south pole is so different from anywhere on Earth.

- Everything runs in the browser. No install and no account.

What we hope to achieve

A tool that a CLPS or Artemis planner could really open during a schedule review, and that a classroom can also use. Next steps would be ground station schedules, relay satellites, north pole terrain and thermal estimates.

Tools

TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js with our own GLSL shaders, astronomy-engine. Python with SpiceyPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow and tifffile for the data pipeline. Vitest for tests. GitHub for hosting.
